power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .20", "p = .30"), Sentence = c("After removing these effects, even the unstandardized analysis reported in Mariano et al. no longer produced a significant effect (p = .20).", "We did not find a significant overall effect in standardized effects, either (p = .30)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 8 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (8). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 284 columns across 19 data files.
#### Issues Identified

44 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 19 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Mariano et al.'s (2025) meta-analysis tested whether people feel a stronger sense of agency (SoA) over actions when they lead to positive outcomes.
The meta-analysis concluded that positive outcomes (e.g. rewards) elicit a stronger implicitly measured SoA than negative outcomes (e.g., punishments).
This pattern is sometimes attributed to a selfserving bias (Takahata et al., 2012).

If such a bias truly exists in implicit measures of SoA, then it could mean that people's reluctance to take responsibility for negative outcomes, such as harm or losses, is less intentional and more fundamental than one might assume.
However, we identify methodological issues in Mariano et al.'s meta-analysis that cast doubt on their core finding.

Our re-analysis addressed these issues and found that, after adjusting for publication bias toward significant results, whether an outcome is negative or positive did not affect people's implicitly measured SoA over their actions.

Caution is needed before interpreting this result to mean that outcome valence does not affect SoA in general, because there is considerable debate about the validity of implicit SoA measures (e.g., Buehner & Humphreys, 2009).

Analysis of standardized effects found no evidence of an outcome valence effect on TC once correcting for publication bias.

Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) compared only a positive or negative condition with a neutral condition.
After excluding these ineligible studies, even Mariano et al.'s original analysis of unstandardized effects failed to support their headline finding.
We tend to have a feeling or sense that we are in control of our actions and their outcomes.
A commonly used measure of this sense of agency (SoA) comes from people's estimates of the time that passed between their action and its effects (Haggard et al., 2002).

text.text: Recently, Mariano et al. (2025) conducted a meta-analytic review of the literature investigating outcome valence effects on TC.
text.formatted: Recently, <ref type="bibr">Mariano et al. (2025)</ref> conducted a meta-analytic review of the literature investigating outcome valence effects on TC.

text.text: The study comprised three meta-analyses: one on TC for negative outcomes, one on TC for positive outcomes, and one on the difference in TC between positive and negative outcomes.
The third meta-analysis was central to Mariano et al.'s titular claim: that people feel a stronger SoA (as indexed by larger TC), or greater control, over positive rather than negative outcomes.
In this commentary, we detail two issues that call into question the credibility of Mariano et al.'s headline finding.
First, Mariano et al. failed to standardize effects to ensure comparability across studies employing different designs.
Our re-analysis based on standardized effects revealed evidence for the null hypothesis after adjusting for publication bias.

Second, the authors included several studies in their meta-analysis that either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only positive or only negative outcomes (i.e., no comparison between them).
Removing these studies made the unstandardized effect (as reported in Mariano et al.) no longer significant.

text.text: We used GPT-5 and 6 (via OpenAI Codex) to partially generate plot code and to debug analysis code.
Meta-analyses are typically conducted on standardized effects (e.g., Cohen's d) to enable comparisons across studies using different designs and measures.
While meta-analyses can use unstandardized effects when all studies report outcomes on the same scale (e.g., weight in kilograms), this does not hold for Mariano et al.'s study.
That all of the TC effects are in the same unit (milliseconds) does not mean they are on the same scale with respect to SoA, which is the underlying construct of interest.
In other words, TC values from one experimental setup might not imply the same SoA as another.
For example, the variability of both perceived and produced intervals increases with interval duration (e.g., Ivry & Hazeltine, 1995), and this alone may affect TC if intervals differ across studies.

text.text: In experiment 2 of Moreton et al.'s study, the stimuli were human faces with positive expressions, yielding a TC of 14.8ms.
In experiment 4, stimuli were sounds with positive connotations, yielding a TC of 280.ms.

Because these experiments did not vary in any other dimension that Mariano et al. coded (e.g., how predictable they were), it seems implausible that the sound stimuli genuinely elicited around 18 times more agency than the face stimuli.
This disparity was more likely due to differences in the stimulus modality across experiments 2.

text.text: This analysis produced moderate evidence against the effect (BF01 = 4.93), a much smaller overall estimate of gz = -.002 (95% CrI [-0.082, 0.070]), moderate evidence in favour of publication bias (BFpb = 6.42), and moderate evidence against heterogeneity (BFfr = 7.19).
Our re-analysis also raised two major data integrity issues.
First, the authors imputed missing SDs for studies, citing Furukawa et al. (2006) as supporting this procedure.
text.formatted: First, the authors imputed missing SDs for studies, citing <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Furukawa et al. (2006)</ref> as supporting this procedure.

text.text: A re-analysis without effects with imputed SDs still produced a significant overall outcome valence on TC (gz = -.09, t(17.8) = -2.6, p = .018).

But RoBMA-PSMA again produced moderate evidence against the effect (BF01 = 3.11), a much smaller overall estimate of gz = -0.012, 95% CrI [-0.117, 0.046], moderate evidence in favour of publication bias (BFpb = 3.77), and moderate evidence against heterogeneity (BFfr = 3.29).
The second issue concerns how Mariano et al. coded and included studies.
Their abstract states that TC was larger for positive than negative outcomes, implying their delta TC meta-analysis was conducted on the difference in TC between these outcome valences.
But a closer look at the included studies reveals that over half of the 64 effects (from 21 articles) included are not comparisons between positive and negative conditions.

Seven effects (from four articles) came from studies that did not manipulate outcome valence at all, but manipulated whether the outcomes were self-related (Chiarella et al., 2020; Hari et al., 2023; Makwana & Srinivasan, 2019; Muth et al., 2024).

text.text: Four effects (from one article) came from designs without a negative outcome (Bu et al., 2022), and 23 effects (from six articles) came from designs without a positive outcome comparison; negative outcomes were compared to either less negative or neutral outcomes (Beck et al., 2017; Borhani et al., 2017; Caspar et al., 2018 Caspar et al., , 2021;; Hayashida et al., 2024; Moretto et al., 2011).

text.text: After removing these effects, even the unstandardized analysis reported in Mariano et al. no longer produced a significant effect (p = .20).
We did not find a significant overall effect in standardized effects, either (p = .30).

RoBMA-PSMA yielded moderate evidence against the effect (BF01 = 7.13), a very small overall estimate of gz = -0.009, 95% CrI [-0.033, 0.176], weak evidence in favour of publication bias (BFpb = 1.34), and moderate evidence against heterogeneity (BFfr = 5.01).
Our reanalysis suggests that, once standardizing effects and accounting for publication bias, there is no difference in the magnitude of TC for negative versus positive outcomes.
Further, once excluding ostensibly ineligible studies from Mariano et al.'s dataset, the outcome valence effect was no longer significant even for unstandardized effects.

Incidentally, standardizing effects revealed another issue with Mariano et al.'s conclusions. Mariano et al. descriptively analyzed studies that produced the largest reverse valence effects (i.e., larger TCs for negative versus positive outcomes) to argue that outcome type (e.g., economic versus emotional) might moderate the effect of valence on TC.

Mariano et al. descriptively</ref> analyzed studies that produced the largest reverse valence effects (i.e., larger TCs for negative versus positive outcomes) to argue that outcome type (e.g., economic versus emotional) might moderate the effect of valence on TC.

text.text: First, this approach conflicts with the fact that the authors did not find that outcome type significantly moderated the valence effect on TC, and our re-analysis also found no significant heterogeneity between effects.
These between-study differences are therefore better explained by sampling error.
Second, the relative differences between the discussed studies change substantially when effects are standardized (Figure 2).

text.text: Not only were these effects relatively small when standardized (gs < .2), but several other studies produced larger reverse effects.

text.text: Critically, our standardized effect analysis found evidence against heterogeneity in the delta TC meta-analysis.
This means that differences in effect sizes between studies are better explained by sampling variance than methodological factors.

Therefore, Mariano et al.'s discussion, which offers a post hoc account that "moral, physical, and social salience" (p. 36) might reverse the outcome valence effect, should be taken with caution, given the lack of evidence for systematic heterogeneity in effect sizes.
We note two additional concerns that future analyses should address.
First, while Mariano et al. combined publications using the Libet clock and interval estimation paradigms, these have been shown to produce TCs of different magnitudes (e.g. Siebertz & Jansen, 2025).

text.text: While standardizing effects puts them on the same scale, it does not account for true differences in effects (i.e., differences in SoA) between different designs.
Task type should therefore be entered as a covariate in moderator analyses to account for the possibility that it is confounded with moderators of interest (e.g. outcome type).
Second, there are differences across studies used in Mariano et al. in how TC is computed.
In most of the included studies, authors first calculate the difference between the actual and reported interval durations for each experimental condition.

They then compare the resulting values between an active, free-choice condition and some baseline comparison condition (ideally, a passive condition that matches the task on all other dimensions) to arrive at TC.
The critical comparison with respect to the TB effect as a proxy for SoA is the difference between acting (in an active condition) and not acting (in a passive comparison condition).
Thus, the inferences one can draw from a given TC effect depend as much on the chosen comparison condition.

To drive home this point, it should be noted that the included study by Chiarella et al. (2020), for example, only included active conditions, in which participants always pressed a key that caused one of three possible shapes to appear after some time interval.

(2020)</ref>, for example, only included active conditions, in which participants always pressed a key that caused one of three possible shapes to appear after some time interval.

text.text: Participants then estimated the interval and reported whether the shape belonged to them, a close friend, or a stranger (with the associations being created during an initial training).

In this case, differences in TC for one's own versus others' shapes might be explained by differences in how the shapes are encoded in memory, which may then result in differences in TC (as just one possible explanation).
Because the study did not include a passive baseline condition (i.e., a no-action condition), it is impossible to discern the extent to which changes in TC related to SoA.
This example highlights the importance of choosing an appropriate experimental and baseline condition.
In short, our re-analysis of Mariano et al.'s data shows that there is likely no outcome valence effect on SoA.

text.text: Interestingly, the question of outcome valence effects on agency was also addressed in a recent meta-analysis by Zhao et al. (2025), who analyzed standardized effects and found that TC was larger for positive outcomes.
text.formatted: Interestingly, the question of outcome valence effects on agency was also addressed in a recent meta-analysis by <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Zhao et al. (2025)</ref>, who analyzed standardized effects and found that TC was larger for positive outcomes.

text.text: However, although Zhao et al. report a significant one-sided comparison (β = 0.38, p = .028) between TCs for positive and negative outcomes, the two-tailed 95% CI for the estimate crosses zero [-0.01, 0.78].

text.text: While the authors did not find evidence of publication bias, their publication bias analysis was conducted on TC effects rather than delta TC effects.

This does not account for the kind of publication bias where authors do not report studies in which positive outcomes do not yield greater TC than negative outcomes, even if TC in both conditions is significant.
It is clear that further research -perhaps in the form of high-powered registered replications -is needed before conclusions about outcome valence effects on SoA can be drawn with confidence.
